rows.selection_reason: No experiments have been completed, so there is zero evidence to exploit. The most important first step is to establish a clean, interpretable baseline. config_001 (rna_only, singleprofile, pca_n2000) is the simplest configuration in the search space: a single modality, a single profile, and a non-learned linear encoder. This provides a reference performance level against which every subsequent design choice (multiprofile aggregation, learned RNA encoders, adding the image modality, fusion strategy) can be measured for marginal contribution. Starting here reduces uncertainty about the floor of the performance landscape and ensures that later multimodal or more complex results are not over-interpreted without a single-modality anchor. It is also the least computationally expensive option, preserving budget for more complex configurations later.

1) Evidence/uncertainty: Only one experiment is complete (config_001: rna_only, singleprofile, pca_n2000 → acc 0.485, F1 0.464). We have no information about whether the image modality carries useful signal, making it impossible to judge whether multimodal fusion is worth the added complexity. 2) What this tests: config_010 (image_only, singleprofile, resnet50) is a clean unimodal ablation that directly measures the standalone predictive power of the image branch. Because it mirrors config_001's singleprofile setting and uses the 'default' encoder for its modality (resnet50 ↔ pca_n2000), the comparison isolates the modality effect. 3) Why best next experiment: Under a tight budget, the single most consequential design question is whether the image modality adds information beyond RNA. If image_only substantially outperforms or underperforms rna_only, it immediately reshapes the search (e.g., prioritize multimodal with the stronger modality, or deprioritize image encoders entirely). This one experiment reduces the largest source of uncertainty and will make every subsequent multimodal or encoder-choice experiment far more interpretable, making it the highest-information-value use of the next slot.

Evidence: Only two experiments are complete. config_001 (rna_only, singleprofile, pca_n2000) achieves 48.5% acc, establishing RNA as the dominant modality. config_010 (image_only, resnet50) achieves only 20.8% acc, showing image is very weak. Critical uncertainty: we have no data on whether multiprofile (vs singleprofile) provides meaningful signal, and this axis affects every downstream configuration. Question tested: Does aggregating multiple cell profiles (via avgpool) with the same PCA-2000 RNA encoder improve over the single-profile baseline? config_002 is directly comparable to config_001, isolating the profile-setting + aggregation variable. Why best next experiment: With only 2 data points, the highest-value information is resolving whether the multiprofile branch of the search space is worth pursuing at all. A positive result opens a large, promising sub-space (configs 002-009, 018-051); a null result lets us prune it and focus budget on encoder and fusion choices. It is a low-variance, clean A/B comparison that maximally reduces uncertainty per experiment.

Evidence: config_002 (rna_only, multiprofile, pca_n2000, avgpool) achieved 0.591 acc, a large jump over config_001 (singleprofile, 0.485), confirming that multiprofile aggregation is a major design lever. Image-only (config_010, 0.208) is very weak, so the near-term gains will come from optimizing the RNA pipeline. Uncertainty: We do not yet know whether transformer aggregation outperforms simple average pooling for combining multiple profiles; this choice will propagate to every future multiprofile experiment (including multimodal). What this tests: config_003 is a clean single-variable comparison to config_002 (avgpool → transformer, all else identical), isolating the aggregation mechanism. Why best next: It directly extends the strongest result, resolves a design decision that affects all downstream multiprofile and multimodal configurations, and if transformer wins it immediately reshapes the search space; if it does not, it confirms avgpool sufficiency and avoids wasting budget on transformer variants later.

Evidence: RNA-only multi-profile with PCA n2000 + avgpool (config_002) is the clear best at 0.591 acc, while image-only ResNet50 (config_010) is very weak at 0.208 acc. Avgpool outperforms transformer (0.591 vs 0.519). The critical open question is whether multimodal fusion can improve upon the strong RNA baseline, given that the image signal from ResNet50 is extremely weak. Config_018 (multimodal, multiprofile, PCA n2000, ResNet50, avgpool, concat) directly tests this: it pairs the best-validated RNA setup with the image modality using the simplest fusion mechanism. If concat fusion with a weak image signal cannot beat 0.591, it strongly suggests image (at least via ResNet50) is not contributing useful complementary information, redirecting budget toward RNA encoder exploration (scvi, scgpt). If it does help, it justifies investing in stronger image encoders (ViT-L) and more sophisticated fusion. This is the highest-information experiment because it resolves a fundamental architectural question (is multimodal worth pursuing?) before committing further budget to that branch.

Evidence: config_018 (multimodal, multiprofile, pca_n2000, resnet50, avgpool, concat) is the best result so far at 0.619 acc / 0.610 F1, showing that multimodal fusion with concat adds ~2.8% over the best RNA-only setup (config_002, 0.591). The fusion strategy (concat vs. weighted) is the one design dimension in this otherwise-validated configuration that has not been tested. Question: Does weighted fusion outperform simple concatenation when combining the (relatively weak) image features with the (strong) RNA features? If the image modality contributes a small but complementary signal, weighted fusion could down-weight it appropriately and avoid diluting the RNA signal; conversely, concat may already be sufficient. Why this is the best next experiment: It is a clean single-variable change from the current best configuration, directly exploiting the strongest evidence while testing an unexplored design axis. The expected performance delta is small but the information gain is high—ruling in or out weighted fusion lets us fix that dimension and focus remaining budget on larger-uncertainty choices (RNA encoder, image encoder) in subsequent experiments.

Evidence: The current best is config_019 (multimodal, multiprofile, pca_n2000, resnet50, avgpool, weighted) at 0.639 acc. The image modality in isolation is very weak (config_010: 0.208 acc with resnet50), yet multimodal still outperforms RNA-only (0.591), suggesting the image adds some signal. However, we have only tested one image encoder (resnet50), which is a relatively basic CNN. The imagenet_vit_l encoder is a substantially more powerful pretrained vision model and is completely untested. Question: Does upgrading the image encoder from resnet50 to imagenet_vit_l improve multimodal performance, or is the image modality's contribution fundamentally limited regardless of encoder quality? Why this is the best next experiment: config_025 is a clean single-variable ablation from the current best (config_019 → config_025, changing only image_encoder from resnet50 to imagenet_vit_l). This directly tests whether the image encoder is the bottleneck in the multimodal pipeline. The result will either unlock a new performance ceiling (if ViT-L helps) or confirm that the image modality's contribution is capped (if it doesn't), both of which are critical for deciding whether to invest further in image-related design choices (aggregation, fusion) or pivot toward RNA encoder improvements (scvi, scgpt).

Evidence: RNA is the dominant modality (0.591 RNA-only vs 0.208 image-only), and our best config (config_019, acc=0.639) uses pca_n2000 as the RNA encoder. However, we have zero evidence on whether a learned/non-linear RNA encoder (scgpt or scvi_n200) could improve over linear PCA. This is the highest-leverage untested design axis since RNA drives most of the signal. Question: Does replacing PCA with the pre-trained generative scgpt encoder improve multimodal performance, holding all other settings at their known-best values (multiprofile, resnet50, avgpool, weighted fusion)? Why this is the best next experiment: config_043 is a clean single-variable swap from config_019, so any performance delta is attributable to the RNA encoder. A positive result would justify further exploration of learned encoders across all multimodal configs; a null or negative result would confirm PCA sufficiency and redirect budget toward other axes (e.g., transformer aggregation in multimodal, or singleprofile multimodal). This maximizes information gain per experiment under the limited budget.

Evidence: The current best (config_019, acc=0.639) uses pca_n2000 + resnet50 + avgpool + weighted fusion in a multimodal multiprofile setup. We have strong evidence that avgpool > transformer for aggregation (0.591 vs 0.519 in RNA-only) and weighted > concat for fusion (0.639 vs 0.619), and that pca_n2000 >> scgpt (0.639 vs 0.525). However, scvi_n200 has never been tested in any experiment. Question: Can a learned variational encoder (scvi_n200) match or beat PCA in the multimodal setting, or is the scgpt failure (0.525) indicative that learned RNA encoders are generally inferior to PCA here? Why this is best: config_031 is a direct single-variable comparison to config_019 (only RNA encoder changes from pca_n2000 to scvi_n200), cleanly isolating the encoder effect. Resolving this uncertainty is critical because if scvi_n200 is competitive, it opens a new optimization axis; if not, we can confidently lock in PCA and focus remaining budget on other dimensions. This is more informative than re-testing transformer aggregation (already strongly disfavored) or swapping image encoders (resnet50 vs ViT showed negligible difference).

Evidence: config_031 (scvi_n200, resnet50, multiprofile, avgpool, weighted) is the best result at 0.678 acc, showing scvi_n200 substantially outperforms pca_n2000 (0.639) and scgpt (0.525) as the RNA encoder. For the image side, resnet50 and ViT-L were nearly equivalent with pca_n2000 (0.639 vs 0.635), but that comparison was made with a weaker RNA encoder. Question: Does upgrading the image encoder to ViT-L provide additional benefit when paired with the stronger scvi_n200 RNA encoder, potentially shifting the modality balance? This is a single-variable change from the current best, keeping all other settings (multiprofile, avgpool, weighted) at their validated optimal values. It is the best next experiment because it directly exploits the strongest evidence while testing the one remaining unexplored interaction (best RNA encoder × best image encoder), and the outcome—whether ViT-L helps or not—will clarify whether further image-side improvements are worthwhile under the limited budget.
